opus-5.5.text:
I think Huadong's early bet meant a lot to us, and not just because of the money. When we started working on synthetic data and simulation, most people in the market didn't see it as a real category. The mainstream view was that data comes from the real world: you collect it, label it, and scale it up, and simulation is a nice research tool but not a business. So in those early conversations we were really asking an investor to believe in something that hadn't been proven yet.

What I appreciated about Huadong was that they didn't push us to explain everything in short-term commercial terms. They asked the hard technical questions. How close can the sim-to-real gap get? Where does synthetic data clearly beat real data, and where doesn't it? Who would actually pay for this in the next two or three years? But underneath that there was a basic conviction that as models got bigger and real-world data got more expensive, harder to collect, and more constrained by privacy and safety, generated data would become infrastructure. That matched what we believed, and it's rare to find an investor who shares your thesis before the evidence is in.

Looking back, I'd describe it as an investment in a direction more than in a product. Our product changed several times. Early on we thought the main use cases would be one set of industries, and later we found the real pull came from others, especially embodied intelligence and robotics, where you just can't gather enough edge cases in the physical world. Huadong gave us room to make those adjustments without treating every pivot as a crisis.

Of course, early capital also comes with pressure. When someone backs you that early, you feel responsible for proving them right. There were stretches where the market wasn't ready and we wondered whether we were too early. But I think being early in this field turned out to be an advantage. We built the toolchains, the rendering and physics pipelines, and above all the understanding of what makes synthetic data useful rather than just pretty. That kind of accumulated know-how is hard to catch up on quickly.

So my overall view is that it was a forward-looking bet, and it gave us the time to do slow, foundational work in an industry that usually rewards speed. I'm grateful for that, and I think the way the field has developed since then has largely borne out the judgment.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I'd say Huadong's investment came at a moment when almost nobody wanted to hear the words "synthetic data." This was before the data bottleneck became an obvious topic. Most investors we talked to at the time thought the interesting problem was models, not data. Their view was that data was something you scraped or bought, and that if you had enough compute and a good enough architecture, the rest would take care of itself.

Huadong saw it differently. I remember our first real conversation with them, and the question they asked wasn't "what's your model" but "what happens when the internet runs out." That was the question we had been obsessing over ourselves. For embodied intelligence in particular, for robotics, there is no internet to scrape. The data doesn't exist. You have to manufacture it, either in simulation or through very expensive real-world collection. So when someone on the other side of the table already understood that framing, it changed the nature of the whole relationship. They weren't betting on us as a trend. They were betting on a thesis about where the constraint would be.

The second thing I'd say is that they were patient in a way that mattered a lot. Synthetic data and simulation have a long validation cycle. You can't show a nice demo in month three. You have to prove that models trained on your data actually transfer to reality, and that takes iteration, and a lot of the early iterations fail in ways that look bad on a slide. Huadong understood that the sim-to-real gap was the real product, not the renderer, not the generator. They gave us the room to be wrong for a while.

And honestly, part of what they gave us was conviction when we doubted ourselves. There were a couple of stretches where we considered pivoting to something more conventional, because the fundraising environment was telling us to. They pushed back. Not in a controlling way, but they kept reminding us why they had invested in the first place.

So how do I view it? I think it was one of the few genuinely contrarian early bets in this space, and the market has moved toward their view rather than away from it. I'm grateful for it, but more than gratitude, I think it validated the idea that in this field, being early on the right question is worth more than being on time with the fashionable answer.

Synthetic data and simulation are about creating a way to test, learn, and improve without depending entirely on what you can collect in the real world. But the key is whether that synthetic data and those simulations actually reflect the problems you need to solve. From my perspective, the value of Huadong’s early investment was giving us room to pursue that work and demonstrate its practical value.
